t.1.73.1: Then, when the night had passed, the great sage Viśvāmitra took leave of the two kings and went to the northern mountain.
t.1.73.2: When Viśvāmitra had departed, King Daśaratha took leave of the Vaideha, the lord of Mithilā, and then swiftly set out for his own city.
t.1.73.3: Then the king of the Videhas, the lord of Mithilā, gave abundant wealth as the bride's gift, many hundreds of thousands of cows.
t.1.73.4: He gave the finest woollen blankets and crores of linen garments, and a fourfold host of elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers, divine in appearance and splendidly adorned.
t.1.73.5: The father of the maidens gave them peerless female and male servants, along with a wealth of gold and fine gold, of pearls and of coral.
t.1.73.7: The lord of Mithilā entered his own dwelling, Mithilā; and the king, lord of Ayodhyā, likewise set out with his great-souled sons.
t.1.73.6: Supremely delighted, the king gave an unsurpassed dowry for the maidens; and having given abundant wealth, the king took leave of the other ruler of the earth.
t.1.73.8: Placing all the sages at the front, he set out with his army and his followers. And as that tiger among men went on his way, together with the host of sages and with Rāghava...
t.1.73.9: Fearsome birds uttered cries here and there, and all the beasts that roam the earth moved around them, keeping them on their right.
t.1.73.11: Having heard these words of King Daśaratha, the great sage spoke in a sweet voice: "Let it be heard what the fruit of this is."
t.1.73.10: Seeing them, the tiger among kings questioned Vasiṣṭha: "The birds are inauspicious and dreadful, and yet the beasts pass by on the right. What is this that makes the heart tremble? My mind is sinking in despair."
t.1.73.12: A terrible danger has arisen, a divine one, issuing from the mouths of the birds; but these beasts are allaying it, so let this anguish of yours be cast aside.
t.1.73.13: As they were conversing there, a wind arose, shaking the whole earth and bringing down the beautiful trees.
t.1.73.14: The sun was covered by darkness, and all the directions did not shine; everything was covered with ash, and that army was as if bewildered.
t.1.73.15: Then Vasiṣṭha and the other ṛṣis, and the king together with his son, remained there as if still conscious; everything else was senseless.
t.1.73.16: In that dreadful darkness, the army, as though covered with ash, beheld one of fearsome appearance, bearing a circle of matted locks.
t.1.73.17: Unassailable like Mount Kailāsa, unbearable like the fire of the world's dissolution, blazing as it were with splendor, he was hard for ordinary people to look upon.
t.1.73.19: Seeing him, terrible in appearance and blazing like fire, all the sages, the brahmins headed by Vasiṣṭha who were devoted to muttered prayer and fire-offerings, gathered together and then spoke among themselves.
t.1.73.18: With an axe slung upon his shoulder, and holding a bow like a mass of lightning flashes and a foremost arrow, he appeared like Hara, the destroyer of Tripura.
t.1.73.20: Surely he who resents his father's slaying will not destroy the kṣatriyas? Having formerly wrought the slaughter of the kṣatriyas, his wrath is gone and his fever spent; surely he does not wish to destroy the kṣatriyas again.
t.1.73.21: Having spoken thus and taking up the guest-offering, the ṛṣis addressed the Bhārgava, terrible to behold, with sweet words: "Rāma, Rāma!"
t.1.73.22: Having accepted that worship offered by the sages, the mighty Rāma Jāmadagnya then addressed Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
